draft.title: Readings and interpretations
card: An interpretation is an argued view of what a text means. It is more than a personal opinion, because it has reasons behind it.
A text can support more than one valid reading. Two readers can reach different views and both be sound.
A reading is valid only when it is backed by close evidence from the text, such as word choices, events and structure.
A reading that ignores or contradicts the text is weak, even if the reader feels strongly about it.
draft.remember: A good interpretation is an argued view, and the text itself supplies the proof.

a.q: Which statement best describes an interpretation of a text?
opts: An argued view of meaning, backed by the text
A personal feeling that needs no support
A summary of the events in order
The one meaning the author intended
a.why: An interpretation is a view of meaning that is argued and supported by evidence from the text. A summary only retells events, so it does not argue a view.
a.clue: Think about what turns a view into an argument.

b.q: Two students read a story in which a girl keeps a locked box she never opens. Sam argues it shows her fear of the past. Priya argues it shows her hope for the future. Each cites lines about the box. What can be said about the readings?
opts: Both can be valid if the evidence supports each
Only one can be valid, because a text has one meaning
Neither is valid, because readers differ
Both are valid whatever the text says
b.why: More than one reading can be valid when each is supported by close evidence from the text. Both are not valid automatically: a reading still has to rest on the text.
b.clue: Both students use evidence from the text.

a.best: An argued view of meaning, backed by the text

b.best: Both can be valid if the evidence supports each
